pages.text: Sociology Standards Sociology Standards Skip Navigation Sociology Standards The U.S. Census Bureau’s Statistics in Schools (SIS) activities are based on relevant education standards and guidelines that outline the foundational knowledge and skills students should have at certain levels. The SIS activities — which are designed to supplement or guide, not replace, existing curricula — help develop these skills and knowledge. Not all educators use the same standards. For this reason, many of the activities address multiple standards and guidelines. SOCIOLOGY American Sociological Association’s National Standards for High School Sociology Published in 2015, these standards are designed to assist teachers and administrators who want to develop high-quality, developmentally appropriate introductory sociology courses over one semester for students in ninth through 12th grades. These standards are organized by four learning domains; each represents a broad area of sociological knowledge and study appropriate for high school. Soil & Groundwater Remediation During a Groundwater University site tour at the Santa Susana Field Laboratory, Josh Mengers, federal project director for the Energy Technology Engineering Center, shows an educational model to demonstrate some of the work being done at the site. The Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Environmental Management (EM) manages one of the largest groundwater and soil remediation efforts in the world. The inventory at the EM sites includes 6.5 trillion liters of contaminated groundwater, an amount equal to about four times the daily U.S. water consumption, and 40 million cubic meters of soil and debris contaminated with radionuclides, metals, and organics. EM’s Office of Subsurface Closure is working with EM site managers around the country to help find solutions to their specific technical issues. At the large sites such as Hanford, Savannah River and Oak Ridge, the Office of Subsurface Closure has conducted research and demonstration projects to test new technologies and remediation approaches. The primary goal of the Office of Subsurface Closure is to expedite closure of major soil and groundwater sites and waste units. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Sonoran Desert National Monument The saguaro cactus is the iconic symbol of the Sonoran Desert and the monument is a place to see extensive forests of the classic cactus. But the monument has more to offer, including distinctive mountains rising from the desert floor. It has three distinct mountain ranges: the Maricopa, Sand Tank, and Table Top mountains, as well as the Booth and White hills, all separated by wide valleys. You can hike or ride horseback almost everywhere in the monument. Four designated trails in three congressionally designated wilderness areas total 26 miles. Many miles of roads are available for mountain biking and motorized vehicle tours. The monument has significant archaeological and historic sites, and remnants of several important historic trails, including the Juan Bautista de Anza and Butterfield Overland national historic trails. Maltijae Pass is a long, winding road in Boeun-gun, North Chungcheong Province, South Korea. Photograph by Jun Michael Park, National Geographic By Martin Zatko Published October 21, 2025 There’s no doubt about it— South Korea is one of the world’s “it” destinations. The country’s new-found mega-popularity has found itself propelled by the music, films, and drama series of the “ Korean Wave ,” whose ripples only seem to increase in size every year. Even before visiting, many also find themselves addicted to Korea’s famously spicy cuisine, with dishes such as bibimbap and japchae —as well as side-dishes like kimchi , and alcoholic drinks such as soju and makgeolli —becoming increasingly popular worldwide. While Seoul and Busan are as modern as cities come, Korea is also a proudly traditional land, with unique culture and customs resulting from its two-millennium-long chain of unbroken dynastic rule. What was once known as the “Hermit Kingdom” has now well and truly crawled out of its shell, but the country remains sprinkled with Buddhist temples and hermitages, especially around its pine-covered mountains.

Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Southwest District Office The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) Southwest District manages about 1.75 million surface acres of public land comprised of the Gunnison , Tres Rios , and Uncompahgre field offices in Colorado. The district includes several specially designated areas — Gunnison Gorge National Conservation Area and Wilderness ; Canyons of the Ancients National Monument (along with its associated Visitor Center and Museum ); the Powderhorn Wilderness Area ; and the southern portion of Dominguez-Escalante National Conservation Area , including the Dominguez Canyons Wilderness. The Spring Creek Basin Wild Horse Herd Management Area is located within the Disappointment Valley in Tres Rios Field Office. The district encompasses approximately 7.26 million acres of subsurface minerals, including the natural gas wells of the Northern San Juan and Paradox basins and coal leases in the valley of the North Fork of the Gunnison River. The Southwest District is home to some of the most spectacular scenery in Colorado. pages.description: For the first time in International Space Station history, all eight docking ports aboard the orbital outpost are occupied following the reinstallation of Northrop Grumman’s Cygnus XL cargo spacecraft to the Earth-facing port of the station’s Unity module. pages.text: SpaceX Starship megarocket blasts off before expected return for reuse | SpaceX | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launches from Starbase in Boca Chica, Texas, on Friday. Photograph: Ricardo Arduengo/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launches from Starbase in Boca Chica, Texas, on Friday. Photograph: Ricardo Arduengo/AFP/Getty Images SpaceX SpaceX Starship megarocket blasts off before expected return for reuse Flight 15 expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over 22 hours, before company catches it at Starbase, Texas Uwa Ede-Osifo Fri 13 Nov 2026 19.53 EST First published on Fri 13 Nov 2026 18.38 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google SpaceX’s Starship megarocket blasted off from Texas on Friday afternoon as the aerospace company sought to make history with a double catch of its reusable rocket, but ultimately fell short. Starship, the world’s largest rocket, standing at 407ft, is expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over the course of 22 hours, before the company catches the rocket at its launchpad at Starbase in south Texas . The rocket, which is on its 15th flight, is composed of two elements: the lower booster, with 33 Raptor engines that fired off during takeoff, and the Starship at the top. As smoke plumes wafted from the launch site, SpaceX employees erupted into cheers. SpaceX had planned for both components to return to its tower, but the booster, named Super Heavy, was aborted, and splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico. The 171ft (52-meter) bullet-shaped upper stage descended into the clutch of the tower’s mechanical arms, ending a 22-hour mission where the craft orbited Earth 14 times. Starship’s 15th test flight was envisioned as a historic double-catch mission, where all parts of the rocket would be returned intact to the launch site, rather than recovered from the ocean as with some previous test flights. The hulking spacecraft is comprised of two parts: a lower booster stage called Super Heavy, whose Raptor engines powered the orbital ascent, and an upper stage also called Starship. Those double-catch ambitions were dashed on Friday, when the booster diverted a few minutes after takeoff and exploded in the Gulf of Mexico. pages.text: Spain 2-3 England: How did Thomas Tuchel's side win and what was learned from Argentina defeat? - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, James Trafford (right) kept Spain out in the latter stages By Emlyn Begley BBC Sport journalist Published 16 November 2026 England held on to beat Spain 3-2 with a backs-to-the-wall finale in the Nations League to finish top of their group. But many observers would have been feeling a sense of deja vu from the World Cup semi-final when England sat back and were beaten by Argentina . So what was different this time? BBC Sport has a look. Were the situations the same? First of all the context of the two games was entirely different. England were 1-0 up against Argentina in the 55th minute on neutral territory in Atlanta - and still had all their players. Anthony Gordon had put them ahead but Lionel Messi set up Enzo Fernandez and then Lautaro Martinez late on. But against Spain the best performance of Thomas Tuchel's reign had them 3-0 up through goals from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White. Elliot Anderson then fouled Lamine Yamal for a penalty, which Mikel Oyarzabal scored - and that began the siege at a partisan Riyadh Air Metropolitano. Nico Williams made it 3-2 but Spain could not find an equaliser, thanks in part to England keeper James Trafford. "Half an hour feels like two hours against a team like this [with 10 men]," Tuchel told ITV afterwards. "That's the way it is. pages.text: Spain 2-3 England: Three Lions produce best win under Thomas Tuchel - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Harry Kane scored for a record-equalling seventh England away game By Phil McNulty Chief football writer in Madrid Published 15 November 2026 Thomas Tuchel went with bold words when reminded about the caution that sabotaged England's World Cup hopes and left them with so much to prove against Spain in the Nations League on Sunday. In a media theatre at the Metropolitano in Madrid, head coach Tuchel's sixth sense led him to go public with what he was convinced England would produce against the world champions. Tuchel looked his inquisitors in the eyes and declared: "We are up for something spectacular." To say Tuchel and England kept their word was a masterpiece of understatement after the finest night of the head coach's reign resulted in a 3-2 victory that was large parts magnificent, some parts madness - and all parts spectacular. It also ended Spain's 43-game unbeaten run - setting aside their penalty shootout defeat by Portugal in the 2025 Nations League final. If England and Tuchel could be accused of being cowed by pressure when they led Argentina in the ill-fated World Cup semi-final, they were thrillingly positive in this unforgiving Madrid environment. pages.text: Spain v England: How Unai Simon became world's best goalkeeper - BBC Sport By Guillem Balague BBC Sport columnist Published 15 November 2026 Peter Schmeichel handed Unai Simon the Yashin Trophy and the room applauded warmly. Then the world's best goalkeeper spent his time talking about everybody else. Simon thanked his parents and his brother. He thanked his girlfriend for being an "oasis of tranquillity", and the friends from home who remind him that "many of us in this room are privileged". 'La cuadrilla', the gang of lifelong friends that is a traditional part of Basque culture, has a WhatsApp group of its own, and he takes them on holiday every summer. He thanked his coaches and team-mates. Like Simon, none of them are regulars on the covers of the media. Then he talked about a man who could not be in the room at last month's Ballon d'Or ceremony in London, but whose influence lives on - Simon's youth academy mentor Koldo Asua, who died in 2021. The Spain and Athletic Club number one is not your archetypal superstar. In fact, he is the complete opposite. He stays away from the headlines and is relatively low profile when compared with some of the game's other goalkeepers. His position as Spain's number is regularly questioned - as was the decision to name him as the world's best. In the part-beauty pageant election that is the Ballon d'Or, being low key can work against you, but the case on the pitch is easy to state - even though it rattles those who see the Premier League as the highest standard reachable. Spectrum sharing optimizes the use of the airwaves, or wireless communications channels, by enabling multiple categories of users to safely share the same frequency bands. Spectrum sharing is necessary because growing demand is crowding the airwaves . Smartphones and appliances, military and public safety radios, wearable devices, smart vehicles and countless other devices all depend on the same wireless bands of the electromagnetic spectrum to share data, voice and images. What is NIST’s Role? As the nation’s measurement authority, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) develops measurement tools, data and methods to make fair, efficient spectrum sharing possible. This work supports not only the trillion-dollar U.S. telecommunications industry and its hundreds of millions of customers but also the U.S. military, which has spectrum in the 3.5-gigahertz (GHz) frequency band that is a focus of pioneering U.S. spectrum-sharing efforts . pages.description: In the 1950s, one couple braved sandstorms and land mines to cross the world's most famous desert.
pages.text: Speeding across the Sahara on one of Earth's most punishing road trips | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE FROM THE VAULT Speeding across the Sahara on one of Earth's most punishing road trips In the 1950s, one couple braved sandstorms and land mines to cross the world's most famous desert. Mark Thiessen By Jinx Rodger Photographs by George Rodger, Magnum Published June 1, 2026 This story originally published in the May 1958 issue of National Geographic magazine. This feature is presented as originally created and may contain stereotypes or negative depictions. See more digitized stories from our archives here . There are several ways to reach the Sahara, depending upon the bank balance, boldness, and backbone of the traveler. You can fly from Algiers and within a few hours be riding a camel through the palmeries of El Goléa or sitting atop the high dunes of In Salah. You can start by train from Algiers or Oran to Colomb Béchar, then hook a ride with a friendly trans-Sahara truck going south—if you don't mind squeezing into a confined space and hearing your teeth rattle for a week or a month. We drove, surrendering our car and ourselves to one of the most punishing trips on earth: more than 4,000 miles in 90 days. And for the Sahara, that's speeding. My husband had crossed the Sahara twice before, during World War II, over compass routes of his own from Chad to Benghazi and then back again through Kufra Oasis to Khartoum. The Sahara beckoned, as it does to anyone who has ever fallen under its spell. And so, naturally, he had to return. I went along as ballast. B

pages.title: Spiders may lure male fireflies to their death with a call of love | National Geographic
pages.description: A new study suggests orb-weaving spiders may manipulate the flashes of male fireflies caught in their web to mimic the mating call of a female.
pages.text: Spiders may lure male fireflies to their death with a call of love | National Geographic ANIMALS Spiders may lure male fireflies to their death with a call of love A new study suggests orb-weaving spiders may manipulate the flashes of male fireflies caught in their web to mimic the mating call of a female. A male firefly is caught in the web of an orb-weaving spider, Araneus ventricosus . Researchers believe that these spiders may manipulate the bioluminescent signals that fireflies use to find mates. Photograph by Xinhua Fu By Gennaro Tomma Published August 19, 2024 Spiders have evolved an impressive array of hunting techniques—from trapping their prey with spit to building webs strong enough to capture snakes. Now, researchers have discovered a particularly malicious tactic that some orb-weaver spiders might use to trick fireflies into their webs. A new study published in Current Biology found that some spiders seem to manipulate the flashing signals of male fireflies they’ve ensnared in their webs to mimic the signals of a female. This glittering call of love attracts other male fireflies to the spider’s web, just like a siren song attracts sailors to death. ( These spiders lure their prey in very crafty ways .) The idea that spiders would put off a meal to use their prey as bait is in itself intriguing, says Dinesh Rao, a researcher at the Universidad Veracruzana who reviewed the paper but wasn’t involved in the study. “Spiders are always hungry, right? So to say, ‘Okay, I'm not going to eat this firefly now and I'll wait for the next one’, it’s […] very interesting.” B

In reality, fingerprints are a two-dimensional representation of a very three-dimensional object. NIST’s work on contactless fingerprint capture standards and tools prompted researchers to step back and take another look at fingerprints — specifically, the way they look before making a 2D impression of them. This image shows one of the test fingerprint ridge patterns that NIST researchers studied while working on contactless calibration targets. Each of the beautiful, majestic rolling hills below is only about 300 to 400 micrometers wide, and all of them together are what makes up your fingerprints. Hoogerheide/NIST Just how long do free-floating neutrons live on average? This electromagnetic proton trap at the NIST Center for Neutron Research (NCNR) is part of an effort to answer that question. Free neutrons break down into other particles — a proton, an electron and an antineutrino — in about 15 minutes on average. This process gives us insight into the weak nuclear force, which governs radioactive decay as well as fusion inside stars. And if neutrons decayed a bit more quickly, the chemical makeup of the universe might be so different that life on Earth would not exist. A better measurement of the neutron lifetime would give physicists greater clarity about the way our universe works. One measurement method is to send a beam of cold neutrons through the electromagnetic trap, which traps protons that emerge from the neutrons’ decay. This video clip, produced using a technique called laser light sheet imaging, shows how microscopic particles can become airborne — and spread throughout the space you’re in — just from opening or closing a package.
